# Exercise 1.3 — When the patients change {#sec-shift}

**60 minutes · pairs, then plenary**

## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Evaluate a fixed model on data it was not trained on, without refitting it.
- Distinguish a change in **who the patients are** from a change in **how the
  outcome arises**, using evidence from the data rather than the story.
- Say which of the two a given model can survive, and why.
- Name the one kind of shift you can detect without ever seeing an outcome.
:::

## The situation

Your model from @sec-pipeline went into use. Twelve months later three monthly
extracts arrive from the data warehouse: `extract_A.csv`, `extract_B.csv`,
`extract_C.csv`, 400 admissions each, same three columns.

Nobody tells you what happened in between. Exactly one of these is true of each
extract:

| | |
|---|---|
| **no shift** | same patients, same relationship. The model should still work. |
| **covariate shift** | the patients changed — $P(X)$ is different — but the relationship between predictors and outcome, $P(Y \mid X)$, is unchanged. |
| **covariate and concept shift** | the patients changed *and* the relationship changed. |

: {tbl-colwidths="[28,72]"}

That distinction is the exercise, so be clear before you start. *Covariate
shift* means you are being asked about different people. *Concept shift* means
the rules moved: the same patient would now have a different length of stay. A
model is a frozen claim about $P(Y \mid X)$. When only $P(X)$ moves the claim may
still be true. When $P(Y \mid X)$ moves it is false, and no amount of data about
the new patients will tell you so unless you also have their outcomes.

## The model you are testing

Each page of this booklet is a fresh session, so the cell below rebuilds the
model exactly as you fitted it in @sec-pipeline — same data, same seed. Run it,
then leave it alone. **Do not refit it on the new extracts.** The whole point is
that the model is frozen and the world moved.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(ggplot2)
library(parsnip); library(rsample); library(yardstick)

los <- read_csv("data/los_data.csv")
set.seed(42)
split   <- initial_split(los, prop = 0.8)
los_fit <- linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm") |>
  fit(LOS ~ Age + Severity, data = training(split))

test_mae <- mae(bind_cols(predict(los_fit, testing(split)), testing(split)),
                truth = LOS, estimate = .pred)$.estimate
round(test_mae, 2)   # your reference number from Exercise 1.2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 3.42
```


:::
:::


## Worked example — extract A


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
A <- read_csv("data/extract_A.csv")
preds_A <- predict(los_fit, new_data = A) |> bind_cols(A)
mae(preds_A, truth = LOS, estimate = .pred)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>   .metric .estimator .estimate
#>   <chr>   <chr>          <dbl>
#> 1 mae     standard        3.58
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-warning}
## The error that will cost you ten minutes
`predict()` on a `parsnip` fit wants `new_data =`, with an underscore. Passing
`newdata =` silently predicts on the training data and returns the wrong number
of rows.
:::

## Task 1 — Did performance survive?

Compute the MAE of the frozen model on all three extracts, with the test MAE
above as the reference. Four numbers, in a table.

::: {.panel-tabset}

mae_on <- function(d) {
  mae(bind_cols(predict(los_fit, new_data = ______), d), truth = LOS, estimate = .pred)$.estimate
}
c(test = test_mae, A = mae_on(A), B = mae_on(B), C = mae_on(C)) |> round(2)

## Task 2 — Did the patients change?

Compare the distribution of `Age` and of `Severity` in each extract against the
original. A summary table and a plot.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
combined <- bind_rows(
  los |> mutate(source = "original"),
  A |> mutate(source = "A"), B |> mutate(source = "B"), C |> mutate(source = "C")
)

combined |> group_by(source) |> summarise(______)

ggplot(combined, aes(x = Age, fill = source)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.35) + labs(x = "Age (years)")
```
:::


::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}

Write down which extracts have a different case-mix from the original. This
question has a clean answer, and it is not the same as the answer to Task 1.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Make it a number, not an impression
Density plots are a good way to see a shift and a bad way to report one. Add one
quantitative statement per extract — the difference in means expressed in
standard deviations of the original, or the proportion of new patients outside
the 1st–99th percentile range of the training ages. "The curves look different"
is not a finding.
:::

## Task 3 — Did the rules change?

This is the task that settles the exercise. For each extract, **refit** a linear
model on that extract alone and compare its coefficients with the original. You
are no longer asking how well the old model predicts; you are asking whether the
relationship it encodes is still the relationship in the data.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
coefs <- function(d) coef(lm(LOS ~ Age + Severity, data = d))
rbind(original = coefs(los), A = ______, B = ______, C = ______) |> round(2)
```
:::


::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
coefs <- function(d) coef(lm(LOS ~ Age + Severity, data = d))
rbind(original = coefs(los), A = coefs(A), B = coefs(B), C = coefs(C)) |> round(2)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>          (Intercept)  Age Severity
#> original       -8.41 0.93     3.44
#> A              -9.67 0.95     3.46
#> B              -8.33 0.95     3.25
#> C               4.61 0.13     1.60
```


:::
:::

:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck on how to judge "different"?
Compare each coefficient against the spread of the original estimate. A change
from 0.93 to 0.95 is noise; a change from 0.93 to 0.13 is not. To be precise,
put a confidence interval round the original with `confint(lm(LOS ~ Age +
Severity, los))` and ask whether the extract's estimate falls inside it.
:::

Classify each extract as `"none"`, `"covariate"` or `"concept"`.

Before you look: write one sentence per extract naming **which piece of evidence
settled it**. If your evidence is "the MAE was high", you have not done Task 3.

## The result that should bother you

One extract contains patients unlike anything in the training data — markedly
younger, markedly sicker — and the frozen model predicts their length of stay
about as accurately as it predicted the original test set.

Five minutes on why, because the reasoning transfers.

1. The model is a straight line in age and severity, and the true relationship in
   that extract is the *same* straight line. Asking it about a 25-year-old is
   asking it to extrapolate, and a correctly specified linear model extrapolates
   correctly.
2. So covariate shift is not inherently harmful. It is harmful when the model is
   wrong in exactly the region the new patients occupy — which you cannot check,
   because you had no patients there.
3. Which is why "the input distribution has shifted" is a reason to look, not a
   verdict. Stretch 1 shows a model for which the same shift is damaging.

::: {.callout-important}
## The asymmetry to remember
You can detect covariate shift with no outcomes at all — age and severity arrive
with the referral. You cannot detect concept shift without outcomes, because it
is a statement about the relationship between inputs and outcome. In a deployed
clinical model the outcomes arrive weeks or months late, so the dangerous shift
is the one you learn about last [@finlayson2021].
:::

## Reflection

Answer in writing; this is the assessable part.

1. Which extract would be most dangerous in clinical use, and why? "The one with
   the worst MAE" is only right if you can say why worst-MAE is the right
   criterion here.
2. Your model is in use. You see `Age` and `Severity` for every new referral, and
   true length of stay only after discharge. Which of the three situations could
   you detect *this week*, and which would you learn about in three months?
3. A colleague proposes refitting monthly on the most recent extract. Name one
   problem this solves and one it creates.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**The key.** A = no shift (the control: a fresh draw from the original
population, original coefficients). B = covariate shift only (age mean moves
from ≈60 to ≈27, severity from ≈5.4 to ≈7.3; coefficients unchanged).
C = covariate **and** concept shift (same new case-mix as B, but the generating
coefficients change from intercept −8.5 / Age 0.94 / Severity 3.37 to
intercept +4.0 / Age 0.15 / Severity 1.60 — an age effect that has essentially
vanished, as if early supported discharge had been introduced).

**Observed numbers.** Linear model MAE ≈ 3.6 on A, ≈ 3.5 on B, ≈ 22.7 on C,
against a test MAE of ≈ 3.4. Refitted coefficients: A and B recover Age ≈ 0.95
and Severity ≈ 3.3–3.5; C returns Age ≈ 0.13, Severity ≈ 1.60.

**Where the class divides.** Most students call B the dangerous one, because the
case-mix change is the visible thing. Hold a show of hands before the reveal.
The moment the B result lands — unfamiliar patients, unharmed predictions — is
the moment the distinction becomes real rather than terminological.

**Reflection answers.** (1) C, because the error is roughly six times the margin
by which the model beat its baseline, and it is systematic: it over-predicts,
which in capacity planning means beds held empty and in discharge planning means
patients told the wrong thing. (2) B and C are both detectable this week from
inputs alone; A is confirmed as "no shift" only once outcomes arrive. The crucial
point: input monitoring cannot tell B from C, and B needs no action while C needs
the model withdrawn. (3) Monthly refitting tracks concept shift automatically,
but it destroys the stable reference against which you detect that anything
changed, it silently learns any feedback loop the model itself created, and the
model in use on 1 March is not the model that was validated.

**Timing.** If short, cut Task 2's plots (keep the summary table) and the
stretches. Never Task 3.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — The same shift, a different model
Refit @sec-pipeline's **decision tree** on the original training data and run it
on all three extracts. Linear regression lost nothing on the covariate-shifted
extract; the tree roughly doubles its error. Explain why, in terms of what a tree
does outside the range of its training data — then say which model you would
rather deploy, and under what monitoring.

(Ours: tree test MAE ≈ 5.9, A ≈ 5.9, B ≈ 9.9, C ≈ 29.9.)
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — Design the monitoring
Specify what the hospital should monitor monthly to catch this automatically.
Five lines: what is measured, on what data, compared with what reference, what
threshold triggers a look, and who looks. Specific enough for a data engineer to
build. Then mark your own specification against the one thing it cannot catch.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 3 — Read one of these
Futoma and colleagues argue that generalisability as usually claimed in health ML
is a myth, and that models should be validated where they will be used
[@futoma2020]. Yang and colleagues measured it across hospital sites for
COVID-19 screening [@yang2022]. Read one; bring a sentence connecting it to
extract C.
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that this model's accuracy depends on an assumption you can state
precisely — that $P(Y \mid X)$ is the same in deployment as in training — and
that you can test it when outcomes are available and partly monitor it when they
are not.

**Cannot:** that a model surviving all three extracts is safe to deploy. These
extracts contain the shifts we built into them. Real services shift in ways
nobody simulated, including in response to the model itself.
